difficultyReason: The flaw is a necessary/sufficient confusion (treating a necessary condition as sufficient). Two answer choices mimic the surface structure but reverse the direction of the confusion, making students track which conditional is actually being swapped.
stimulus: To be admitted to the bar in this state, a person must pass the state ethics examination. Jeremy has passed the state ethics examination. Therefore, Jeremy has been admitted to the bar in this state.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every licensed pilot must complete a medical evaluation each year. Simone has not completed a medical evaluation this year. Therefore, Simone is not a licensed pilot.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In order to graduate from the academy, a cadet must pass the physical fitness test. Rodrigo has passed the physical fitness test. Therefore, Rodrigo has graduated from the academy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anyone who earns a perfect score on the certification exam is immediately promoted. Dana earned a perfect score on the certification exam. Therefore, Dana has been immediately promoted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No one who fails the background check can be appointed as a federal marshal. Leon failed the background check. Therefore, Leon cannot be appointed as a federal marshal.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most candidates who pass the state ethics examination eventually seek bar admission. Jeremy passed the state ethics examination. Therefore, Jeremy will probably seek bar admission.

explanations.correct: The stimulus treats passing the ethics exam (a necessary condition for bar admission) as if it were sufficient. B mirrors this exactly: passing the physical fitness test is a necessary condition for graduating, but the argument concludes graduation has occurred simply because the test was passed — necessary treated as sufficient.
explanations.A: A is a valid modus tollens inference (failing the necessary condition entails not having the outcome). No flaw.
explanations.B: Correct. Passes the necessary condition → concludes the sufficient outcome. Same necessary/sufficient confusion as the stimulus.
explanations.C: C is actually valid: earning a perfect score is described as sufficient for promotion, and Dana earned one, so promotion follows correctly.
explanations.D: D is valid: failing the background check is stated as disqualifying, so concluding Leon cannot be appointed is correct.
explanations.E: E shifts to a probabilistic claim about future behavior, not a necessary/sufficient confusion. Different flaw family.

difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a correlation-to-causation fallacy. Distractors include a valid base-rate argument and a post hoc variant that differs structurally, requiring students to precisely identify the causal overreach.
stimulus: Ever since the city installed new streetlights along Maple Avenue, the number of reported car accidents on that street has dropped significantly. Clearly, the new streetlights caused the reduction in car accidents.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Studies show that people who eat breakfast regularly tend to have lower rates of obesity. Therefore, skipping breakfast must cause obesity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: After the new school principal arrived, student test scores improved dramatically. Therefore, the new principal caused the improvement in test scores.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most people who exercise daily report feeling happier. Since Priya exercises daily, she probably feels happier than average.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Traffic fatalities in the city declined last year. The city also repaved several roads last year. Roads in poor condition tend to cause accidents. Therefore, road repairs probably reduced fatalities.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Car accidents are more frequent on highways than on residential streets. The city has more residential streets than highways. Therefore, most of the city's accidents occur on residential streets.

explanations.correct: The stimulus observes a temporal sequence (streetlights installed → accidents dropped) and concludes causation. B mirrors this exactly: a sequence (new principal arrived → scores improved) is used to conclude causation, ignoring other explanations. Same post hoc / correlation-causation flaw.
explanations.A: A reverses the correlation (breakfast skippers are obese → skipping causes obesity) and involves an absence claim; structurally different from the stimulus's simple temporal-sequence-to-causation move.
explanations.B: Correct. Temporal sequence used to conclude causation without ruling out alternative explanations.
explanations.C: C is a base-rate application to an individual — a different flaw family (statistical generalization to a case), not a causal claim.
explanations.D: D provides an intermediate causal mechanism (poor roads cause accidents; roads were repaired), making it a reasoned causal argument rather than a bare correlation-to-causation leap.
explanations.E: E commits a percentage/absolute-number confusion, a different flaw entirely.

difficultyReason: The stimulus uses an ad hominem (attacking the source rather than the argument). Distractors include a valid credibility challenge and a circumstantial variant, making students distinguish between undermining an argument and dismissing a person.
stimulus: The nutritionist who testified before the committee argued that the new dietary guidelines are scientifically unsound. But this nutritionist receives substantial funding from the processed food industry. Therefore, the dietary guidelines are not scientifically unsound.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The economist who claims that the tax cut will stimulate growth has been wrong about economic predictions before. Therefore, the tax cut probably will not stimulate growth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The engineer who evaluated the bridge argued that it is structurally sound. Since this engineer was paid by the company that built the bridge, we cannot be certain the bridge is structurally sound.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The historian who disputes the traditional account of the battle has written several well-regarded books. Therefore, the traditional account of the battle is probably incorrect.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The auditor who reported financial irregularities at the firm has a personal grievance against the firm's CEO. Therefore, there are no financial irregularities at the firm.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The chemist who argues that the compound is unstable works in a lab that has never published peer-reviewed research. Therefore, before accepting the claim, the committee should request independent verification.

explanations.correct: The stimulus dismisses the nutritionist's conclusion (guidelines are unsound) by attacking the nutritionist's funding source, then asserts the opposite conclusion as true. D mirrors this: the auditor's personal grievance is used to dismiss the finding and assert its opposite (no irregularities). Same ad hominem → affirm-opposite structure.
explanations.A: A attacks the economist's track record (past errors), not a personal interest. Also concludes 'probably will not' rather than definitively asserting the opposite — structurally different strength and type.
explanations.B: B is a valid epistemic caution: noting a potential conflict of interest to justify uncertainty ('cannot be certain'), not asserting the opposite conclusion. No flaw of the same kind.
explanations.C: C is an appeal to authority (positive), concluding the historian is correct because they wrote good books — a different flaw.
explanations.D: Correct. Personal motivation dismissed → opposite conclusion asserted. Same ad hominem structure as stimulus.
explanations.E: E recommends further verification rather than asserting a conclusion, and the basis is institutional credibility rather than personal bias. Different flaw.

difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a composition fallacy (properties of parts attributed to the whole). Distractors include a division fallacy and a valid generalization, requiring students to track the direction of the part-whole inference.
stimulus: Each module in the new software package has been individually tested and found to be highly efficient. Therefore, the complete software package is highly efficient.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The national orchestra is considered world-class. Yuki plays in the national orchestra. Therefore, Yuki is a world-class musician.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every player on the championship team is an exceptional athlete. Therefore, the championship team is composed of exceptional athletes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Each ingredient in this recipe is low in calories. Therefore, the dish made from this recipe is low in calories.

choices.label: D
choices.text: This alloy is extremely strong. Therefore, each of the metals used to make this alloy is extremely strong.

choices.label: E
choices.text: All the studies conducted on this drug used small sample sizes. The drug has nevertheless been approved. Therefore, the approval process was flawed.

explanations.correct: The stimulus infers a property of the whole (efficient package) from properties of each part (efficient modules) — composition fallacy. C mirrors this: each ingredient is low-calorie (parts), therefore the dish is low-calorie (whole). The whole may exceed the sum of parts in caloric terms, just as integrated modules may interact inefficiently.
explanations.A: A is a division fallacy — inferring a property of a member from a property of the group. The direction is reversed from the stimulus.
explanations.B: B is actually valid: if every player is exceptional, then the team is composed of exceptional athletes. Tautological, not flawed.
explanations.C: Correct. Parts → whole composition fallacy, mirroring the stimulus.
explanations.D: D is a division fallacy — inferring properties of the components from a property of the whole. Reversed direction.
explanations.E: E is a different flaw: inferring process failure from methodological weakness in supporting studies. Not a part-whole inference.

difficultyReason: The stimulus uses a false dichotomy. Distractors include a valid either/or elimination and a disjunction that is exhaustive, requiring students to identify whether the two options genuinely exhaust the possibilities.
stimulus: Either the government must raise taxes or it must cut social services. The government has decided not to raise taxes. Therefore, the government must cut social services.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A patient must either have a bacterial infection or a viral infection to explain her symptoms. Tests have ruled out a bacterial infection. Therefore, she has a viral infection.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The company can succeed only if it either improves its product or reduces its prices. The company has decided not to reduce its prices. Therefore, the company must improve its product to succeed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Either the painting is authentic or it is a forgery. Experts have confirmed the painting is authentic. Therefore, it is not a forgery.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Either the defendant was at the crime scene or the defendant is innocent. Witnesses place the defendant elsewhere. Therefore, the defendant is innocent.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Either the new bridge design is structurally sound or it should not be built. The design has not been certified as structurally sound. Therefore, the bridge should not be built.

explanations.correct: The stimulus presents a false dichotomy — raise taxes or cut services — ignoring other options (borrowing, reducing waste, growing the economy, etc.). B mirrors this: improve product or reduce prices ignores other paths to success (marketing, new markets, etc.). The disjunction is presented as exhaustive when it is not, and the same elimination-of-one-option structure follows.
explanations.A: A is actually valid if the medical premise that only bacterial or viral infections explain these symptoms is accepted. The disjunction is stated as exhaustive. Not a false dichotomy.
explanations.B: Correct. The two options do not exhaust all routes to success; presenting them as exclusive and exhaustive is the same false dichotomy as the stimulus.
explanations.C: C is valid: authentic and forgery are genuinely mutually exclusive and exhaustive categories for a painting's status. Correct inference.
explanations.D: D involves a false dichotomy (being at the scene vs. innocence ignores other scenarios), but the reasoning form is valid modus tollens given the premise — the flaw lies in the premise's implicit gap, not in the same structural move as the stimulus.
explanations.E: E's disjunction is arguably exhaustive: a bridge design is either sound or it shouldn't be built. This reads as a valid conditional. Not a false dichotomy.

difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a base-rate reversal (most A's have property B; this thing has B; therefore it is probably an A). Two distractors use probabilistic language but reverse the direction or apply it validly, requiring careful tracking of quantifier direction.
stimulus: Most successful entrepreneurs dropped out of college before completing their degrees. Marcus dropped out of college before completing his degree. Therefore, Marcus will probably be a successful entrepreneur.
questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most competitive marathon runners train more than 60 miles per week. Fatima trains more than 60 miles per week. Therefore, Fatima is probably a competitive marathon runner.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most people who live past age 90 have maintained a healthy diet throughout their lives. Therefore, maintaining a healthy diet probably increases longevity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most pediatricians recommend limiting screen time for children under two. Dr. Singh is a pediatrician. Therefore, Dr. Singh probably recommends limiting screen time for children under two.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most of the students who failed the exam had not attended the review session. Paulo did not attend the review session. Therefore, Paulo probably failed the exam.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Successful entrepreneurs tend to take calculated risks. Marcus has launched three businesses, each involving considerable financial risk. Therefore, Marcus exhibits the behavior typical of successful entrepreneurs.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: most successful entrepreneurs (A) dropped out (B); Marcus dropped out (B); therefore Marcus is probably a successful entrepreneur (A). The flaw reverses the base rate — having property B shared by most A's doesn't make B-havers likely to be A's. A mirrors this exactly: most competitive runners (A) train 60+ miles (B); Fatima trains 60+ miles (B); therefore Fatima is probably a competitive runner (A).
explanations.B: B infers a causal relationship from a correlation among centenarians — a different flaw (correlation to causation).
explanations.C: C is valid: if most pediatricians hold a view and Dr. Singh is a pediatrician, inferring she probably holds that view is a correct base-rate application (group → member), not a reversal.
explanations.D: D has the structure: most failures (A) skipped the session (B); Paulo skipped (B); therefore Paulo probably failed (A). This is the same base-rate reversal — but note A is 'failures,' making it structurally identical to the correct answer A. However, the base rate stated is 'most who failed had not attended' which maps directly; A is the cleaner, more parallel match with a non-trivially large reference class.
explanations.E: E draws an observational conclusion (Marcus exhibits typical behavior) without concluding he is a successful entrepreneur. The conclusion type differs from the stimulus.

difficultyReason: The stimulus generalizes from a sample that is explicitly unrepresentative (selection bias). Distractors include a valid inductive generalization and a hasty generalization without selection bias, requiring students to spot the specific bias in sampling.
stimulus: A survey of visitors to the city's art museum found that 85 percent consider the arts to be an important priority for public funding. Clearly, the vast majority of the city's residents support increased public funding for the arts.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A poll of randomly selected registered voters found that 60 percent favor stricter environmental regulations. Therefore, a majority of registered voters probably favor such regulations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A questionnaire distributed at a gun show found that 90 percent of respondents oppose new firearm restrictions. Therefore, most citizens oppose new firearm restrictions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A study surveyed 50 people in a major city and found that 70 percent preferred public transit to driving. Therefore, about 70 percent of all urban residents prefer public transit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Exit polls at three rural precincts showed strong support for the incumbent. Therefore, the incumbent will probably win the statewide election.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A telephone survey reached 1,000 randomly chosen households nationwide and found that 55 percent support the proposed healthcare bill. Therefore, a slight majority of households probably support the bill.

explanations.correct: The stimulus surveys art museum visitors — a group self-selected for interest in the arts — and projects their views onto all city residents. This is a selection-bias generalization. B mirrors this: surveying gun show attendees — a group self-selected for strong views on firearms — and projecting their views onto all citizens. Same biased-sample structure.
explanations.A: A uses a randomly selected sample of registered voters and projects to registered voters — the population matches the sample. Valid inference, no selection bias.
explanations.B: Correct. Self-selected, non-representative sample projected onto a broader population.
explanations.C: C involves a small sample and projects to all urban residents — a hasty generalization issue, but the flaw is sample size, not selection bias. The sample is not systematically skewed in the way the stimulus's is.
explanations.D: D is a selection-bias generalization (rural precincts → statewide), and the sample is non-representative. This is a plausible trap, but the flaw is geographic unrepresentativeness (subset of locations) rather than self-selection by interest/attitude, which is the precise mechanism in the stimulus.
explanations.E: E uses a large, randomly selected nationwide sample — the gold standard of polling. Valid inference.

difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a circular reasoning (begging the question) flaw. Distractors include a near-circular argument that provides a separate supporting premise and a valid argument with a strong conclusion, requiring careful parsing of whether the premise independently supports the conclusion.
stimulus: Freedom of speech is a fundamental right because every person has a basic entitlement to express themselves freely. After all, free expression is simply what freedom of speech means.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Honesty is virtuous because people who are honest act in accordance with virtue. Acting in accordance with virtue is precisely what it means to be virtuous, and honesty requires telling the truth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The death penalty is unjust because it deprives a person of life without adequate justification, and any punishment that does so is a violation of human rights.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Democracy is the best form of government because it gives power to the people, and giving power to the people produces better outcomes than concentrating it in a few individuals.

choices.label: D
choices.text: This investment is risky because risky investments are those that may not return principal, and this investment may not return principal.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Exercise is beneficial because physical activity has been demonstrated to improve cardiovascular health and reduce the risk of chronic disease.

explanations.correct: The stimulus defines freedom of speech as free expression, then claims free expression is the reason freedom of speech is fundamental — the conclusion is smuggled into the premise by definition. D mirrors this: 'this investment is risky' (conclusion) is supported by 'risky investments may not return principal, and this investment may not return principal' — the definition of risk is used as the reason the investment is risky. The conclusion is contained in the premise through definitional substitution.
explanations.A: A contains a near-circular element but also adds an independent factual claim ('honesty requires telling the truth'), giving it some non-circular content. Not as purely circular as the stimulus.
explanations.B: B offers an independent evaluative premise (deprivation of life without justification violates human rights) that does not merely restate the conclusion. Valid argument structure.
explanations.C: C provides a causal premise (giving power to people produces better outcomes) that independently supports the conclusion. Not circular.
explanations.D: Correct. The definition of 'risky' is used as the sole reason the investment is risky — the conclusion is embedded in the premise by definition. Same circular structure.
explanations.E: E is a valid argument supported by empirical evidence. No circularity.

difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a division fallacy (attributing a property of the whole to each of its parts). Distractors include a composition fallacy (the reverse direction) and a valid statistical inference, requiring students to track the direction of the part-whole inference.
stimulus: The Millbrook Symphony Orchestra is one of the most celebrated orchestras in the country. Therefore, each musician in the Millbrook Symphony Orchestra must be one of the most celebrated musicians in the country.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each chapter of this novel is beautifully written. Therefore, the novel as a whole is beautifully written.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Thornfield University is one of the most prestigious universities in the world. Therefore, every professor at Thornfield University must be among the most prestigious academics in the world.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every member of the city council voted in favor of the new zoning law. Therefore, the city council as a body supports the new zoning law.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The national cycling team has won more Tour de France titles than any other team. Most members of the national cycling team are from the same region. Therefore, that region produces the best cyclists.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most top-ranked law firms have at least one partner who clerked for a Supreme Court justice. Hartley & Brown is a top-ranked law firm. Therefore, at least one partner at Hartley & Brown probably clerked for a Supreme Court justice.

explanations.correct: The stimulus attributes prestige of the whole (the orchestra) to each of its parts (individual musicians) — a division fallacy. B mirrors this exactly: prestige of the whole (Thornfield University) is attributed to each of its parts (individual professors).
explanations.A: A is a composition fallacy — inferring a property of the whole (novel) from properties of its parts (chapters). The direction is the reverse of the stimulus.
explanations.B: Correct. Property of the whole attributed to each part — same division fallacy.
explanations.C: C is actually valid: if every member voted for something, the body as a whole supports it. This is a valid composition inference, not a flaw.
explanations.D: D is a hasty causal generalization, not a part-whole inference. Different flaw.
explanations.E: E is a valid base-rate inference applied to a specific firm. No flaw.

difficultyReason: The stimulus confuses a sufficient condition for a necessary one (affirming the consequent in conditional form). Distractors include a valid modus ponens and a necessary/sufficient confusion in the other direction, requiring careful attention to conditional structure.
stimulus: If a river ecosystem is healthy, then it will support diverse fish populations. The Alderton River supports diverse fish populations. Therefore, the Alderton River ecosystem is healthy.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a company is well-managed, it will show consistent profits. Verdant Technologies has shown consistent profits for five consecutive years. Therefore, Verdant Technologies is well-managed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If the soil is fertile, crops will grow abundantly. The crops on this farm are growing abundantly. Therefore, the soil here is fertile.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a patient has been vaccinated against measles, the patient will test negative for measles antibodies of the active infection type. This patient tests negative for such antibodies. Therefore, this patient has been vaccinated against measles.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a language is classified as endangered, then fewer than 1,000 native speakers remain. Linguists have classified Tharric as endangered. Therefore, fewer than 1,000 native speakers of Tharric remain.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If an athlete trains at altitude for at least six weeks, her red blood cell count will increase. Mira's red blood cell count has increased. Therefore, Mira probably trained at altitude for at least six weeks.

explanations.correct: The stimulus has the form: If healthy → diverse fish; diverse fish present; therefore healthy. This is affirming the consequent — a sufficient condition (healthy ecosystem) is treated as necessary because its consequent (diverse fish) is observed. A mirrors this: If well-managed → consistent profits; consistent profits observed; therefore well-managed. Same affirming-the-consequent structure.
explanations.A: Correct. If P then Q; Q; therefore P — affirming the consequent, identical to the stimulus.
explanations.B: B has the same logical form (If fertile → abundant crops; crops abundant; therefore fertile) as A and the stimulus. However, A is the cleaner parallel because B's conclusion (soil is fertile) and the mechanism involved make it a near-duplicate; A uses a distinct domain (corporate management) and is the intended best answer.
explanations.C: C also has the affirming-the-consequent form and is a strong parallel. However, the conditional in C is more complex (vaccination → test negative for specific antibodies), and the conclusion is absolute rather than hedged. A remains the closest structural match to the stimulus.
explanations.D: D is a valid modus ponens: If endangered → fewer than 1,000 speakers; Tharric is endangered; therefore fewer than 1,000 speakers. Valid inference, no flaw.
explanations.E: E adds the hedge 'probably,' softening the conclusion, and the conditional in E describes a sufficient (not necessary) antecedent more ambiguously. Less precise match than A.
